newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan PM fears revolution if system unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan PM fears revolution if system unchanged.

text.p: Pakistan's new Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif on Thursday raised the spectre of a bloody revolution if what he called the prevailing colonial system in the country continued for a few more years.

A statement by his Pakistan Muslim League (PML) party quoted him as telling the party's parliamentary deputies that they had received a mandate for change in last month's elections and his government would not budge an inch from that aim.
"The nation has given us a mandate to change the outdated colonial system that has prevailed for 50 years (since independence from Britain in 1947) and to remove all ills," Sharif said.
"If this system is allowed to stay for a few more years, a bloody revolution can come," he was quoted as saying.

Sharif, whose party won a landslide in the February 3 elections on promises of economic uplift and fighting corruption, said: "We will not budge an inch from our pledge to the nation, otherwise there will be disaster."
He said his government would have to work on a"war-footing" to fight social evils, punish criminals and make basic reforms.
"For this, we will have to take short-term and long-term measures, whose bitterness may be felt for some days but their result will be sweet and pleasing."

Sharif said President Farooq Leghari had told him that Pakistan would have become a defaulter towards international financial institutions if there had been a delay of a few days in dismissing former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto in November.

Leghari dismissed Bhutto's three-year-old government on November 5 on the disputed charges of corruption and misrule by using a controversial constitutional amendment that empowers him to sack a prime minister and dissolve the National Assembly (lower house of parliament).
The parliamentary deputies made proposals to remove "dark aspects of the Eighth Amendment and to establish supremacy of parliament", the statement said without giving details.
The PML and allied parties have won a two-thirds parliamentary majority needed to amend the constitutiton.

A mission of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) now in Pakistan is due to complete a review of the country's economic performance by Friday to decide whether to disburse the next $122 million tranche of a standby loan.
Sharif has pledged to revive industry and stimulate export-led growth to rescue the ailing economy, but some analysts say his priorities may conflict with those of the IMF.
"We will put the economy on rails without caring for pressure of every kind and without compromising principles and taking dictation," the prime minister said in his speech.
Sharif accused Bhutto before the elections of taking dictation from the IMF and the World Bank in formulating economic policies. Bhutto denies the charge.
